name: Iris Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What does a normal site day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a six-person crew replacing doors, windows and kitchens in flats where residents still live. My trade certificate taught the joinery, but experience taught me to explain the mess before a tool comes out. Seeing a warm, finished room makes the stairwell dust worthwhile.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears on you outside the work itself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The low foreperson rate and paperwork. Joel, my partner, drives a delivery van, and our two children are in school; we have a mortgage and about three weeks of expenses saved. I use a chatbot now and then to tidy a snag report, but I check every line before sending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the refurbishment crew that a tidy report is useful, but the old flats still need hands and patience. The chatbot I use now and then can clean up my snag list after I check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel’s van-driving wage and mine barely cover the mortgage and two children’s school costs. We have about three weeks of expenses saved. A quiet AI story does not change the contractor’s tight prices. My foreperson rate stays low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting doors and windows in occupied flats and using the same report tool occasionally. I would ask the housing contractor for the overdue rate review at our next site meeting, with the crew beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even if the machines barely change. I already count the food bill before payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the rate review about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead six people but still earn close to the lower carpentry rate. I want the contractor to put the foreperson rate and start date in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you cut food now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We buy basics already, and the children need proper meals. I would rather make a pay claim with the team than pretend the food bill can vanish.

say: I would tell the crew a **tidy report** cannot replace careful work in occupied flats.
I would request a written **foreperson rate** at the next site meeting.
think: Our **three-week cushion** and low rate keep the mortgage tight even in a mild AI future.
Joel’s **van wage** helps, but food and school costs leave little room.
do: Keep fitting **flat doors and windows** and checking snag reports.
Bring the **rate review** to the site meeting with the crew.
feel: **Anxious** about existing household bills rather than new technology.
S0.quote: A quiet AI story does not change the contractor’s tight prices.
fieldNote: Her baseline money pressure drives the **anxious mood** in a plateau.
The chatbot is already **occasional use**; the concrete new action is a group pay request.

steps.text: Keep fitting occupied-flat doors and checking existing snag reports
Bring foreperson pay claim to the next crew site meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can book materials, but it will not tell an upset tenant why the kitchen is in the hallway. I would insist someone on the crew checks every new schedule with the residents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office staff could be cut, and the contractor might then ask us to finish more flats for the same pay. My hours could shrink between jobs, and three weeks of reserve would not cover a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would try the new AI schedule only after the housing contractor gives us access and shows it works on one occupied block. I would also bring the crew to the union meeting to ask for paid gaps between flats if the schedule creates waiting days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn a screen once it proves useful, but I cannot put a missed week on the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the block trial check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether tenants know the visit time and whether a door arrives in the right size. I would speak to two households before calling the schedule useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first bill at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, if two weeks go unpaid. Joel’s wage covers food and fuel, but not the whole house payment by itself.

say: I would demand **resident checks** before AI schedules occupied-flat repairs.
I would ask the **union meeting** for pay during gaps between scheduled flats.
think: The contractor could demand **more flats** for the same low wage.
Two unpaid weeks could put the **mortgage** at risk despite Joel’s van pay.
do: Learn the new **AI schedule** only after access and a successful occupied-block trial.
Join the **union meeting** to seek pay for waiting days.
feel: **Anxious** about possible unpaid gaps and mortgage pressure.
S1.quote: I cannot put a missed week on the mortgage.
fieldNote: She accepts a proven new screen but insists on **tenant confirmation** first.
The union request concerns **paid waiting days**, a concrete household risk under tighter scheduling.

steps.text: Learn AI scheduling only after access and a successful occupied-block trial
Join union meeting to demand pay for gaps between flats

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI in 2028 can write the timetable, but a person still fits a door beside a family’s dinner table. Robots around 2031 might do the fitting, and residents must have a say in any trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the contractor to reduce some fitting posts when robots can work in flats. I could be one of the people cut, and three weeks of savings will not carry the mortgage while I search the few local sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid refurb shifts and ask the union for written notice before any robot trial in occupied homes. If two monthly rosters lose paid days, I would apply to posted local joinery vacancies, leaving only for a firm wage that covers the mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have a plan on paper. The children cannot eat a plan if the pay packet stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a job far away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a firm offer pays enough to cover travel and the household bills. Joel’s van work is local, and I would not move the children for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should residents be asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether they accept a machine working in their kitchen and who comes back when a door does not close. The first trial should never be a surprise visit.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** writes timetables before 2031 robots fit doors in occupied flats.
I would demand **resident consent** and union notice for any robot trial.
think: I expect **fitting posts** to shrink, and my own role could be cut.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot support a long search while the mortgage continues.
do: Keep **paid refurbishment shifts** while the contractor offers them.
Seek **union notice** before occupied-flat robot trials.
Apply to **posted local joinery jobs** after two reduced rosters, leaving only for mortgage-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** by expected job cuts and a very short cash runway.
S2.quote: The children cannot eat a plan if the pay packet stops.
fieldNote: She anticipates a real **job cut** after capable robots reach occupied flats.
The job search is tied to **posted vacancies** after two reduced rosters and mortgage-covering wages.

steps.text: Keep paid occupied-flat repair shifts while offered
Seek union notice before robot trials in residents homes
Apply to posted local joinery vacancies after two reduced rosters for mortgage-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough to test robots on empty rooms before anyone asks them to work beside tenants. The crew should be paid to show what fails, not used as free demonstrators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 could speed reports, while robots do the hands-on work around 2034. I will be fifty one and still need a wage; with few local jobs, a paid trainer role could help if the contractor actually posts one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the flat crew next year and ask for paid training on robot checks. If the contractor posts a funded trainer vacancy with a wage that covers the mortgage, I would complete the course and apply; otherwise I would keep fitting doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years gives me more room than two. I would rather learn a proven machine than wait for the job to disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train without a posted role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We cannot lose paid shifts for a course with no vacancy behind it. I would need funded fees and paid study hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should an empty-room trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot measuring a crooked frame and stopping before a child could wander into its path. I would ask the crew to write down every failed stop.

say: I would insist on **empty-room trials** before robots enter occupied flats.
I would ask for **paid crew testing** and a real trainer vacancy.
think: I still need **steady pay** in 2034, when capable robots arrive.
A posted **trainer role** could help only if its wage covers the mortgage.
do: Keep leading **flat repairs** next year while paid shifts remain.
Complete **funded robot-check training** only with paid hours and a posted mortgage-covering trainer role.
**Apply** for the posted trainer role after funded training only if its wage covers the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about future work, with a possible funded route if offered.
S3.quote: The crew should be paid to show what fails, not used as free demonstrators.
fieldNote: Her training decision requires **funded fees** plus paid hours and a posted role.
The five-year lead matters, but she still faces **few local vacancies** and current mortgage pressure.

steps.text: Keep leading paid occupied-flat repairs next year
Complete funded robot-check course only with paid hours and posted mortgage-covering trainer role
Apply for posted trainer role after funded course only if wage covers mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew a decade lets us teach apprentices how to work in someone’s home before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. A tenant is not a test object.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty six when robots can fit the work. Joel and I still expect to need both wages, and the three-week reserve we have now will not turn into a cushion by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the crew on occupied-flat repairs during 2026 and add twenty from each paid month to savings if Joel’s van hours and the mortgage payment stay covered. In the first year after 2036 I would compare actual repair shifts and posted local roles; by 2039 I would apply only if a real vacancy pays enough for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our present thin reserve, though ten years makes preparation possible. I want to save from wages we really receive, not from promises about future work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the extra twenty come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From paid months after the mortgage and school costs, not from moving our existing emergency cash. If Joel’s van hours fall, we would pause it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the longer timetable change the children’s schooling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not today. They are still in school, and I would not steer them away from a trade on a prediction alone.

say: I would keep **tenant care** and hands-on apprenticeship in the decade before 2039 robots.
I would explain that **2036 thinking AI** arrives before machines can fit doors.
think: We will still need **both wages** when capable robots reach flats around 2039.
Our **three-week reserve** remains a present worry even with ten years to prepare.
do: Keep **2026 occupied-flat shifts** while paid work continues.
Save an extra **twenty monthly** only if Joel’s hours, mortgage and school bills permit it.
feel: **Anxious** about current cash, with time for gradual preparation.
S4.quote: I want to save from wages we really receive, not from promises about future work.
fieldNote: The new monthly transfer is genuine **new saving** only while both household pay and core bills allow.
Her later job search still needs a **posted mortgage-covering role**, not a course enquiry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could reduce our occupied-flat fitting crew by 2031 while the mortgage has no room to wait. Posted mortgage-covering joinery jobs, funded paid training and union notice would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who explains a robot repair to the person whose kitchen is in pieces. A resident deserves a human answer before the machine enters the flat.

headlineQuote: A resident deserves a human answer before the machine enters the flat.
portrait: **Iris**, 43, leads occupied-flat refurbishment with a trade certificate but low pay and only three weeks saved.
Her partner’s **van wage** helps meet the mortgage and two children’s school costs, while nearby joinery jobs are scarce.
She uses **AI occasionally**, after checking its output, and favours crew bargaining and resident consent.
The **2028 case** worries her because robots could reach fitting work around 2031 before the household has a buffer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her paid flat repairs around 2031 while the mortgage continues.
whatWouldHelp: **Posted mortgage-covering jobs**, paid funded training and union notice would help her respond.
